questions.question: How do @ExceptionHandler and @ControllerAdvice work together for centralised error handling in Spring MVC?
questions.title: @ExceptionHandler and @ControllerAdvice for Centralised Error Handling
questions.direct_answer: **@ExceptionHandler** marks a method that handles a specific exception type; when placed inside a **@ControllerAdvice** class, it applies globally across all controllers in the application, enabling a single, reusable error-handling strategy rather than duplicating catch blocks in every controller.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to design clean, maintainable error handling in a real Spring application rather than scattering try-catch in every controller.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Defining @ExceptionHandler only inside a controller class (local scope) when the requirement is global; also returning HTML error pages from a @RestControllerAdvice instead of a structured JSON error body.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss the difference between @ControllerAdvice and @RestControllerAdvice, mention that you can scope advice to specific packages or base classes, and show how to map exceptions to RFC 7807 ProblemDetail (Spring 6+).

sections.title: Local @ExceptionHandler Catches One Controller — @ControllerAdvice Catches Them All
sections.content:
The most common mistake is defining `@ExceptionHandler` only inside individual controllers, then wondering why error responses are inconsistent across the API. **A local `@ExceptionHandler` has scope limited to the controller it's defined in.** Move it to a `@ControllerAdvice` class and it handles exceptions from every controller.

The resolution order is important: **local handlers take priority over global ones.** If a controller defines its own `@ExceptionHandler(IllegalArgumentException.class)` and a `@ControllerAdvice` also handles the same exception, the local one wins. This lets you override global behavior for specific controllers without changing the advice class.

`@RestControllerAdvice` is the REST-friendly variant — it combines `@ControllerAdvice` with `@ResponseBody`, so handler methods automatically serialize their return value to JSON.
- You can also **scope an advice to specific packages or annotation types** with `@ControllerAdvice(basePackages = "com.example.api")` or `@ControllerAdvice(annotations = RestController.class)`.
- This scoping is valuable in applications that serve both REST APIs and server-rendered pages — different advice classes can return JSON errors for API controllers and HTML error pages for web controllers.

sections.title: Designing the Exception Hierarchy — Business Exceptions, Validation, and the Catch-All
sections.content:
A well-structured error handling strategy has three layers. First, **business exception handlers** for your domain — `ResourceNotFoundException` returns 404, `DuplicateEmailException` returns 409, `InsufficientBalanceException` returns 422. Each maps to a specific HTTP status with a meaningful error message.

Second, a **framework exception handler** for Spring's own exceptions. `MethodArgumentNotValidException` (from `@Valid` failures) should return 400 with a list of field-level errors. `HttpRequestMethodNotSupportedException` should return 405 with the allowed methods.

Third, a **catch-all for unexpected exceptions** that returns 500. This is where the catch-all trap matters — never return 400 from a catch-all, or `NullPointerException` becomes "Bad Request" and you'll never notice the bug. Log the full stack trace and return a generic error to the client.

Spring Boot 3.x supports **RFC 7807 ProblemDetail** as a standard response format — `type`, `title`, `status`, `detail`, and extensible custom fields. Using this standard means all errors follow the same structure without designing a custom schema.

sections.title: RFC 7807 ProblemDetail — The Standard Error Response Body That Clients Can Depend On
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@ControllerAdvice` is global; `@RestControllerAdvice` = `@ControllerAdvice` + `@ResponseBody`** — use `@RestControllerAdvice` so exception handler return values serialize as JSON without additional annotations.
- **Local `@ExceptionHandler` takes precedence over global `@ControllerAdvice`** — when the same exception type is handled both locally and globally, the local handler in the controller wins.
- **Handler method resolution uses the most specific exception type** — `@ExceptionHandler(ConstraintViolationException.class)` wins over `@ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)` when a `ConstraintViolationException` is thrown.
- **`ResponseEntityExceptionHandler` handles Spring MVC internal exceptions** — extend it in your `@ControllerAdvice` and override `handleMethodArgumentNotValid` to customize the `400` response for validation failures.
- **ProblemDetail (RFC 7807, Spring Boot 3.x)** — `ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, "Order 123 not found")` produces a standardized error body; clients rely on predictable structure instead of parsing free-form messages.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Exception handling in Spring MVC has two levels: local handlers inside a controller, and global handlers in `@ControllerAdvice`. Getting the scoping and precedence right is what determines which handler fires for which exception.

**`@ControllerAdvice` scope**
- By default, applies to all controllers in the application
- Narrow the scope: `@ControllerAdvice(assignableTypes = OrderController.class)` or `@ControllerAdvice(basePackages = "com.example.orders")`
- `@RestControllerAdvice` = `@ControllerAdvice` + `@ResponseBody` — the return value of every `@ExceptionHandler` method is written as the response body via `HttpMessageConverter`

**Handler resolution**
- Spring walks the exception class hierarchy to find the most specific matching `@ExceptionHandler`
- Local handler in the originating controller takes precedence over global `@ControllerAdvice`
- Multiple `@ControllerAdvice` beans: order them with `@Order`; lower value = higher priority

**Extending `ResponseEntityExceptionHandler`**
- Extend it in your `@RestControllerAdvice` to get free handling of Spring MVC built-in exceptions: `MethodArgumentNotValidException` (Bean Validation failures), `NoHandlerFoundException` (404), `HttpMessageNotReadableException` (malformed JSON)
- Override the protected methods to customize the response body format

**ProblemDetail (Spring Boot 3.x)**
- `spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true` switches Spring's default error responses to RFC 7807 format automatically
- Return `ProblemDetail` from your `@ExceptionHandler` methods for a standardized, interoperable error format

questions.question: How does RFC 7807 ProblemDetail work in Spring Boot 3, and how do you translate domain exceptions into it consistently?
questions.title: RFC 7807 ProblemDetail in Spring Boot 3
questions.direct_answer: **RFC 7807** defines `application/problem+json` — a small fixed shape (`type`, `title`, `status`, `detail`, `instance`) with free-form **extension members** for context. Spring Framework 6 / Boot 3 ship this as the **`ProblemDetail`** class plus the **`ErrorResponse`** interface; `ResponseEntityExceptionHandler` auto-produces it for the built-in Spring MVC exceptions, and you plug in domain translations via `@RestControllerAdvice` with `@ExceptionHandler` methods that return `ProblemDetail` (or throw an `ErrorResponseException`). Set `spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true` (Boot 3.0+) to make Spring emit ProblemDetail for framework exceptions too. The envelope is the same across validation, auth, domain, and unexpected errors — that uniformity is the whole point.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know RFC 7807 is the IETF standard error envelope, can use Spring 6's `ProblemDetail` and `ErrorResponse` API, wire one `@RestControllerAdvice` to cover domain + framework + fallback, and add extension members (`code`, `traceId`, `errors[]`) without breaking the contract.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Mixing ProblemDetail responses for some endpoints and Spring Boot's legacy `{timestamp, status, error, message, path}` for others — because `spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=false` (the Boot 3 default) leaves framework exceptions on the old shape. Also: using `ProblemDetail.forStatus(...)` without ever setting `type`, so every problem has the default `about:blank` URI and no way to branch on problem class.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the `ErrorResponse` vs `ErrorResponseException` split, `MessageSource` internationalisation of the `title`/`detail`, extending `DefaultHandlerExceptionResolver`, and how Spring 6 auto-maps common MVC exceptions (`MethodArgumentNotValidException`, `HttpMessageNotReadableException`, `MaxUploadSizeExceededException`) into typed ProblemDetail responses when problemdetails is enabled.

sections.title: What RFC 7807 Standardises — and What Spring 6 Adds
sections.content:
RFC 7807 defines a tiny JSON object for HTTP errors: `type` (URI identifying the problem class), `title` (short human summary), `status` (HTTP status), `detail` (longer human message), `instance` (URI of the specific occurrence).
- Any additional keys are **extension members** — implementers' free space for machine-readable context like a stable error code, validation errors, or a trace ID.
- The media type is `application/problem+json`.

Spring Framework 6 / Boot 3 turn this into first-class plumbing:
- **`ProblemDetail`** — a mutable bean with setters for each RFC 7807 field and `setProperty(String, Object)` for extension members
- **`ErrorResponse`** — an interface combining `HttpStatusCode`, `ProblemDetail`, and headers; any exception that implements it automatically gets mapped by Spring
- **`ErrorResponseException`** — a ready-made `RuntimeException` implementing `ErrorResponse`; throw it from any controller and Spring will serialise it
- **`spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true`** — makes Spring emit ProblemDetail for its own MVC exceptions (`MethodArgumentNotValidException`, `HttpMessageNotReadableException`, `NoResourceFoundException`, etc.) instead of the legacy `{timestamp, status, error, path}` shape
- **`ResponseEntityExceptionHandler`** — base class your `@RestControllerAdvice` extends to override any of the built-in translations

The payoff is a single error shape across every code path — framework, validation, domain, fallback — parsed by a single client-side handler.

sections.title: Enabling ProblemDetail + Sample Output
sections.content:
# application.yml
spring:
  mvc:
    problemdetails:
      enabled: true           # framework exceptions -> application/problem+json
  webflux:
    problemdetails:
      enabled: true           # same flag for WebFlux
  messages:
    basename: messages        # for i18n of titles / details

# Without the flag, Spring Boot still returns ProblemDetail for exceptions
# your own @ExceptionHandler methods produce, but framework exceptions
# (e.g. bad JSON body) fall back to the legacy error shape.

# A sample response with the flag enabled:
# HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
# Content-Type: application/problem+json
#
# {
#   "type":   "https://errors.api.acme.com/resource/not-found",
#   "title":  "Resource not found",
#   "status": 404,
#   "detail": "Order ord_abc123 was not found.",
#   "instance": "/v1/orders/ord_abc123",
#   "code":    "ORDER_NOT_FOUND",
#   "traceId": "7a9c3f12b4e84e0a"
# }

sections.title: Domain Exceptions as ErrorResponse — No Advice Needed
Single @RestControllerAdvice Covering Everything
Field by Field — What Each RFC 7807 Key Means
sections.content:
**`type` (URI, required)**
- Identifies the problem class; clients branch on `type`, not status
- Ideally dereferenceable — point at a docs page with cause and resolution
- Default when not set is `about:blank` — a missed opportunity; always set it

**`title` (string, required)**
- Short human summary ("Insufficient funds", "Validation failed")
- Should not change with the specific occurrence — same `type` = same `title`
- Good target for `MessageSource` i18n

**`status` (int, required)**
- HTTP status code as a number in the body — helps older clients that swallow headers
- Must match the response's actual status code

**`detail` (string, optional)**
- Human-readable explanation of this **specific** occurrence ("Balance $12.40, required $50.00")
- Safe for developer tools; not for end users — the UI should use `type` + `code` to pick its own copy

**`instance` (URI, optional)**
- URI of the specific request or occurrence — Spring sets it to the request path by default if you leave it null
- In distributed systems, pair with `traceId` extension for full correlation

**Extension members (free-form)**
- `code` — stable machine-readable enum (`ORDER_NOT_FOUND`); recommended on every response
- `traceId` — correlation with APM/logs
- `errors[]` — field-level validation errors
- Domain-specific context — `balance`, `required`, `resourceType`, `resourceId`
- Never put secrets, stack traces, or SQL in extensions

sections.title: Internationalisation, Security, and Testing
sections.content:
**MessageSource-backed titles and details**
- Spring 6's `MessageSource` can resolve `title` and `detail` per `Accept-Language`
- Use `ProblemDetail.setProperty("titleKey", "order.notFound.title")` + a filter that translates keys to localized text based on the request locale
- Keep the machine-readable `code` language-neutral — always in English SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE

**Security perimeter**
- In auth errors, don't disclose whether the username exists — one `AUTH_INVALID_CREDENTIALS` covers both wrong-user and wrong-password
- In authorization errors, a `404` is sometimes more correct than `403` when revealing resource existence itself is a leak
- Never include raw ORM / SQL exception messages in `detail` — map them to a generic `BODY_MALFORMED` or `INTERNAL_ERROR`

**Testing the advice**
- **MockMvc**: `mockMvc.perform(...).andExpect(status().isNotFound()).andExpect(jsonPath("$.code").value("ORDER_NOT_FOUND")).andExpect(content().contentType("application/problem+json"))`
- **WebTestClient** (WebFlux): same pattern with `webTestClient.get().uri(...).exchange().expectStatus().isNotFound().expectBody().jsonPath("$.code").isEqualTo(...)` 
- Always assert `Content-Type: application/problem+json` — drift here breaks every client

**Observability**
- Log every error the advice translates with `code`, `traceId`, and request path
- Emit a Micrometer counter `http.server.errors` tagged by `code`/`status` — alerting on code-level spikes (e.g. `BILLING_INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS` jumping 20×) often detects real business issues faster than 5xx rates

**Legacy clients**
- If older clients still parse the pre-RFC-7807 shape, an `@RestController` filter can sniff `Accept` and emit the old shape for a window; but this is technical debt you want to retire

**Versioning**
- The envelope is part of the public contract — treat changes to field names or required fields as a breaking change
- Adding new extension members is safe; renaming or removing is not

sections.title: Trade-offs and Common Mistakes
sections.content:
**When RFC 7807 wins**
- New public APIs — IETF standard, Spring-native, mature tooling in clients (`problem-details` libraries in Go, Python, Node)
- APIs consumed by multiple client teams — one envelope reduces cross-team error-handling bikeshedding
- Regulated products needing an auditable error taxonomy

**When a custom envelope may be fine**
- Internal-only APIs already invested in a Stripe-style flat shape
- Narrow microservice with a single consumer — adopting RFC 7807 is still recommended but not urgent

**Mistakes the audit team sees most**
- `spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=false` (the default) — custom advice emits ProblemDetail but framework exceptions return the legacy shape → mixed envelopes on the same API
- `ProblemDetail.forStatus(...)` without ever calling `setType(...)` — every response has `type: about:blank`, so clients can't branch on problem class
- Catching `Exception` once and rebuilding the ProblemDetail from scratch in every controller — violates DRY and invites drift
- Leaking ORM/SQL errors via `ex.getMessage()` — the advice must translate, not echo
- Reusing `code`s across unrelated problems — clients build branches that false-match
- Forgetting to set `Content-Type: application/problem+json` — Spring's `ProblemDetail` + default `MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter` usually gets this right, but custom converters can override

**Performance**
- ProblemDetail is a tiny object — serialization cost is negligible vs business-logic time
- Extension members via `setProperty` are backed by a LinkedHashMap — fine for the few keys a response carries

**Backwards compatibility**
- Bumping from pre-Boot-3 to Boot 3 with `problemdetails.enabled=true` is a visible contract change — coordinate the cutover with clients or stage via media-type negotiation (`Accept: application/problem+json`)

**Interaction with WebFlux**
- `ResponseEntityExceptionHandler` (MVC) has a WebFlux sibling with the same API
- Same `ProblemDetail` class; same flag (`spring.webflux.problemdetails.enabled=true`)
- Reactive chains can throw `ErrorResponseException` directly and the framework serialises it

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **RFC 7807 fields** — `type`, `title`, `status`, `detail`, `instance` + free-form **extension members**; media type `application/problem+json`
- **Spring 6 / Boot 3 support** — `ProblemDetail` bean, `ErrorResponse` interface, `ErrorResponseException`, `ResponseEntityExceptionHandler`
- **Turn on `spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true`** so framework exceptions emit ProblemDetail too — otherwise you have mixed envelopes
- **Always set `type` to a stable URI** — `about:blank` is the default and kills the ability to branch on problem class
- **Extension members carry the contract** — `code` (stable enum), `traceId`, `errors[]` for validation, domain context (`balance`, `required`)
- **One `@RestControllerAdvice` covers everything** — domain `ErrorResponse` exceptions, framework validation/bad-body, auth, and a final `@ExceptionHandler(Throwable.class)` safety net
- **Never leak stack traces or ORM/SQL messages** — translate them into `INTERNAL_ERROR` with a `traceId` pointing to logs
- **Test with MockMvc / WebTestClient** — assert status, `Content-Type`, `code`, and extension members to prevent silent contract drift

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
RFC 7807 is the IETF standard for HTTP error bodies, and Spring 6 turned it into first-class plumbing.

**The envelope**
- Five standard fields: `type`, `title`, `status`, `detail`, `instance`
- Plus free-form extension members — where `code`, `traceId`, and field-level `errors[]` go
- Content-Type is `application/problem+json`

**Spring 6 primitives**
- `ProblemDetail` — mutable bean with setters for each field and `setProperty` for extensions
- `ErrorResponse` — interface any exception can implement to be auto-mapped
- `ErrorResponseException` — ready-made RuntimeException; throw it and Spring serialises it
- `ResponseEntityExceptionHandler` — base class your advice extends to override built-ins

**The one-line fix most projects miss**
- `spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true` — without it, framework exceptions (bad JSON, validation, missing resource) return the legacy `{timestamp, status, error, path}` shape while your custom advice emits ProblemDetail — mixed envelopes on the same API

**Fields I always set**
- `type` URI pointing at docs — never leave it as `about:blank`
- Short `title` — same for every occurrence of this problem class
- `detail` — specific to this occurrence, for developer tools not end users
- `instance` — request path, set automatically by Spring if null

**Extensions I add by convention**
- `code` — stable SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE enum clients branch on
- `traceId` — correlation with APM and logs
- `errors[]` for validation — `{field, code, message}` per field
- Domain context — balance, required, resource IDs

**Single advice covers everything**
- `ErrorResponse` handler stamps `traceId` and `instance`
- `MethodArgumentNotValidException` override emits field-level errors
- `HttpMessageNotReadableException` override for bad JSON bodies
- `AuthenticationException` for 401 with `WWW-Authenticate`
- Final `Throwable` catch-all — logs the stack trace, returns `INTERNAL_ERROR` with `traceId`

**Common mistakes**
- Leaving `spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=false` — mixed envelopes
- Never setting `type` — every response has `about:blank`
- Echoing `ex.getMessage()` in `detail` — leaks ORM/SQL internals
- Rebuilding ProblemDetail from scratch in every controller — DRY violation, drift
- Reusing `code`s across unrelated problems — clients false-match

**Testing**
- MockMvc or WebTestClient assertions on status, `Content-Type: application/problem+json`, `code`, and extension members
- The envelope is public contract; tests prevent silent regressions

questions.question: How do you translate Spring Bean Validation failures (@Valid, MethodArgumentNotValidException) into a structured ProblemDetail response?
questions.title: Validation Error Response Shape
questions.direct_answer: Override **`handleMethodArgumentNotValid`** (and `handleConstraintViolation` for `@Validated` path/query params) in a `@RestControllerAdvice` extending `ResponseEntityExceptionHandler`. Build a **`ProblemDetail`** with `status=400`, a stable `code=VALIDATION_FAILED`, and an `errors[]` extension member containing one entry per field: `{field, code, message, rejectedValue}`. Collect **all** failures — never short-circuit on the first. Use a stable per-constraint code (`NOT_BLANK`, `NOT_EMAIL`, `SIZE_EXCEEDED`) sourced from `FieldError.getCode()` so the client can render per-field messages in its own locale. Apply the same shape across `@Valid` body failures, `@Validated` parameter failures, and Jackson deserialization issues so the client writes one handler.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know which exceptions Bean Validation throws in each context (`@Valid` on @RequestBody, `@Validated` on path/query, class-level validation in services), how to translate them all into one field-level error shape, and why a stable per-constraint code matters for client UX.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Serializing `MethodArgumentNotValidException` directly — the client gets a huge Java-ish object with `target`, `codes`, `arguments`, `bindingResult`, and cryptic `NotBlank.customer.email` keys. Also: returning only the first error, forcing users to fix fields one at a time across multiple round-trips.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss `ConstraintViolationException` vs `MethodArgumentNotValidException`, cross-field validation via `@AssertTrue`/class-level validators, `MessageSource` localization keyed by constraint code, `@Valid` nested collections (`List<@Valid ItemDto>`), and why the `rejectedValue` field matters (and when to scrub it for PII).

sections.title: Where Validation Failures Come From
sections.content:
Spring surfaces Bean Validation failures through three different exception types depending on **where** the validation ran:

- **`MethodArgumentNotValidException`** — thrown when `@Valid` on a `@RequestBody` or `@ModelAttribute` parameter finds field failures. Has a `BindingResult` with `FieldError` entries.
- **`HandlerMethodValidationException`** (Spring 6.1+) — thrown when `@Validated` on a controller method parameter (e.g. `@RequestParam @Min(1) int page`) fails. Replaces the older `ConstraintViolationException` for controller-level parameter validation.
- **`ConstraintViolationException`** — thrown when service-layer validation via `@Validated` on a bean fails, e.g. `@Validated class CustomerService { void create(@Valid CustomerRequest req) { ... } }`.

Clients can't be expected to distinguish these. The job of the `@RestControllerAdvice` is to normalise all three into **one** `ProblemDetail` with an `errors[]` array — each entry a `{field, code, message, rejectedValue}` record. That uniformity is what lets the client write a single render-validation-errors component.

sections.title: DTO with Bean Validation Constraints
Advice — Translating All Three Exception Types
Wire Shape — What the Client Receives
sections.content:
# Request with 3 invalid fields and a nested validation failure
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/v1/customers \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
        "name":"",
        "email":"not-an-email",
        "birthDate":"2099-01-01",
        "address":{"street":"","countryCode":"USA","postalCode":"abc"},
        "phones":[]
      }'

# Response
HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{
  "type":    "https://errors.api.acme.com/validation/invalid-request",
  "title":   "Validation failed",
  "status":  400,
  "detail":  "6 field(s) failed validation.",
  "instance": "/v1/customers",
  "code":    "VALIDATION_FAILED",
  "traceId": "7a9c3f12...",
  "errors": [
    { "field": "name",                 "code": "NOTBLANK", "message": "must not be blank" },
    { "field": "email",                "code": "EMAIL",    "message": "invalid email",
      "rejectedValue": "not-an-email" },
    { "field": "birthDate",            "code": "PAST",     "message": "must be in the past",
      "rejectedValue": "2099-01-01" },
    { "field": "address.street",       "code": "NOTBLANK", "message": "must not be blank" },
    { "field": "address.countryCode",  "code": "SIZE",     "message": "size must be between 2 and 2",
      "rejectedValue": "USA" },
    { "field": "phones",               "code": "SIZE",     "message": "size must be between 1 and 5" }
  ]
}

# Client uses `field` + `code` to render per-field messages in its own locale.
# `message` is for developer tooling; never show it directly to end users.

sections.title: Design Choices That Make the Shape Work
sections.content:
**Stable `code` per constraint**
- `FieldError.getCode()` returns the annotation simple name (`NotBlank`, `Size`, `Pattern`) — uppercase it for a stable enum
- Client can branch per code: `SIZE` → show min/max, `PATTERN` → show expected format, `EMAIL` → show email helper
- Document the full set of codes in your API docs; add-only evolution

**Dotted field paths for nested DTOs**
- `@Valid` cascades into nested objects and collections — `FieldError.getField()` returns dotted paths like `address.street` and `phones[0].number`
- Don't flatten — the dotted path is essential for rendering errors next to nested inputs

**Collect all errors, never short-circuit**
- Bean Validation runs every constraint by default; the advice should surface every failure
- Exception: class-level `@AssertTrue` constraints where later checks depend on earlier fields — use validation groups if you need ordered stops

**`rejectedValue` — carry it, but scrub PII**
- Useful for developer debugging and for UI to highlight the offending input
- Scrub emails, credit-card numbers, and long strings before returning — log/audit logs are the right place for raw values

**Cross-field validation**
- Use class-level validators (`@StartBeforeEnd`, `@PasswordsMatch`) — these surface as `ObjectError` (global error) rather than `FieldError`
- Map them to `field: "_global"` or a synthetic field name agreed with the client

**`@Validated` vs `@Valid`**
- `@Valid` — JSR-380 annotation, triggers cascading validation on `@RequestBody`
- `@Validated` — Spring's annotation, enables method-level validation and validation groups (`@Validated(Create.class)`)
- Use `@Validated` on controllers/services for parameter validation; `@Valid` on fields/params for cascading

**Validation groups**
- Different rules for create vs update — `@NotNull(groups = Create.class)`, then `@Validated(Create.class)` on the endpoint
- Avoid if you can — group sprawl gets painful; prefer separate DTOs

**i18n**
- `@NotBlank(message = "{customer.name.required}")` resolves through `MessageSource`
- Per-request `LocaleContextHolder` picks the locale from `Accept-Language`
- Keep the `code` language-neutral; localize `message` only

sections.title: Gotchas and Anti-patterns
sections.content:
**Serializing the raw exception**
- `MethodArgumentNotValidException` has a huge `BindingResult` with `codes[]`, `arguments`, `target`, and nested Spring types — Jackson by default dumps a 30-field blob
- Always translate in the advice; never return the exception directly

**Short-circuiting on first error**
- Cost: user round-trips once per field; UX is miserable
- Bean Validation runs everything by default — **don't** add early returns in your advice

**Wrong exception for @Validated params**
- Pre-Spring 6.1, this was `ConstraintViolationException` on controller params; Spring 6.1 switched to `HandlerMethodValidationException`
- Handle both if you support older Spring; the advice covers three exception types for a reason

**Jackson deserialization errors aren't bean validation**
- Wrong type in JSON (`"age": "abc"` for `int age`) throws `HttpMessageNotReadableException` (cause `MismatchedInputException`) before Bean Validation runs
- Handle these separately with `code: BODY_MALFORMED`; clients can branch on `code`

**Nested list validation**
- `List<@Valid PhoneDto> phones` — without the inner `@Valid` annotation, elements are not validated
- Field paths come out as `phones[0].number` — preserve the brackets

**Default messages leak into UI**
- `message: "must not be blank"` is a fine developer-tool message, not an end-user one
- Clients should use `field`+`code` to render their own copy; `message` is a fallback

**Locale mismatches**
- `Accept-Language: fr-FR` should localize messages; if your `messages.properties` only has English, clients get English even on a French request — tests often miss this

**Empty `errors[]`**
- Global errors only — surface them anyway with `field: _global` or `_form`; never return an empty array that pretends the failure was status-only

**Testing**
- Fuzz each DTO with invalid payloads and assert the shape; snapshot tests are fine for the envelope structure
- Assert every constraint in the DTO has a handled path; adding a new constraint without a test is the classic regression

sections.title: Trade-offs and Alternative Shapes
sections.content:
**Flat `errors[]` vs map-of-field**
- Flat array `[{field, code, message}]` is the common shape; clients iterate and render
- Map `{email: "invalid", name: "blank"}` is compact but loses per-field `code` and `rejectedValue`
- Dotted paths (`address.street`) work in both shapes but clients with nested forms usually need the array

**Include `rejectedValue` or not**
- Pros: UI can highlight input, devs can debug
- Cons: PII leakage if not scrubbed; may bloat responses
- Compromise: include for non-sensitive scalars, scrub strings above a length or matching PII patterns

**Stable `code` sources**
- Annotation simple name (`NotBlank` → `NOTBLANK`) — simple, auto-derivable
- Custom per-constraint attribute (`@NotBlank(message = "{x}", payload = {Code.NAME_REQUIRED})`) — richer but more code
- Start with annotation name; escalate to custom only if the client needs finer discrimination

**Cross-field error placement**
- `field: _global` — common convention; clients render above the form
- `field: "start"` with message "must be before end" — attaches to one field but misleads about the source of truth
- Choose one convention; document it

**Validation inside service vs at the edge**
- Edge (controller) — fails fast, returns `400`, no service logic runs
- Service (`@Validated` on a bean) — catches programmatic callers too, but throws `ConstraintViolationException` → harder to map consistently
- Standard: validate at the edge for HTTP entry points, re-validate critical invariants in the service when the service is also called from jobs/listeners

**`@Valid` on @RequestBody vs manual validation**
- `@Valid` + advice — idiomatic, testable, uniform
- Manual `Validator.validate(...)` — use only for complex imperative checks or when you need to decide whether to fail or auto-correct

**Error count in `detail` — localize or not**
- `"%d field(s) failed validation."` is fine for a developer-tools detail
- Client locale rendering uses `errors[].code`/`message`, not `detail` — safe to leave English

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Three exception types, one response shape** — `MethodArgumentNotValidException` (@Valid body), `HandlerMethodValidationException` (@Validated params, Spring 6.1+), `ConstraintViolationException` (service-layer) all normalize to the same `ProblemDetail`
- **`errors[]` extension array** with `{field, code, message, rejectedValue}` — the canonical Spring-to-JSON mapping for per-field errors
- **Stable per-constraint `code`** derived from `FieldError.getCode()` (uppercased annotation name) — lets clients branch and localize independently of server text
- **Collect all failures** — Bean Validation runs everything by default; the advice must surface all of them so the user fixes once, not N times
- **Dotted field paths for nested DTOs** — `address.street`, `phones[0].number`; don't flatten
- **Scrub PII from `rejectedValue`** — emails, cards, long strings; the client doesn't need raw values to render errors
- **Don't conflate Jackson errors with validation** — malformed JSON throws `HttpMessageNotReadableException` before Bean Validation; give it its own `code: BODY_MALFORMED`
- **One `@RestControllerAdvice` handles all three paths** plus a fallback — uniformity is the whole point

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring Bean Validation surfaces through three different exception types and my advice normalises them into one response shape.

**The three exception types**
- `MethodArgumentNotValidException` — `@Valid` on `@RequestBody` or `@ModelAttribute`; has a `BindingResult` with `FieldError` entries
- `HandlerMethodValidationException` (Spring 6.1+) — `@Validated` constraints on controller method parameters like `@RequestParam @Min(1) int page`
- `ConstraintViolationException` — `@Validated` on a service bean; raised from Hibernate Validator

Clients shouldn't care which one fired — they all produce the same `errors[]` array.

**The response envelope**
- RFC 7807 `ProblemDetail` with `status=400`, `title="Validation failed"`, `code="VALIDATION_FAILED"`
- Extension member `errors` — array of `{field, code, message, rejectedValue}` entries
- `traceId` extension for correlation with APM and logs

**The `code` convention**
- Uppercase annotation simple name: `NotBlank` → `NOTBLANK`, `Size` → `SIZE`, `Pattern` → `PATTERN`, `Email` → `EMAIL`
- Stable enum clients branch on and localize against; message text is secondary

**Field paths**
- `FieldError.getField()` returns dotted paths — `address.street`, `phones[0].number`
- Preserve them; don't flatten; clients need them to highlight nested inputs

**The `@RestControllerAdvice`**
- Extends `ResponseEntityExceptionHandler`
- Overrides `handleMethodArgumentNotValid` and `handleHandlerMethodValidationException`
- Separate `@ExceptionHandler(ConstraintViolationException.class)` for service-layer failures
- Each path builds the same `errors[]` list and returns the same `ProblemDetail`

**Collecting all failures**
- Bean Validation runs every constraint by default — my advice never short-circuits on the first
- Short-circuiting forces users into N round-trips, one fix at a time; terrible UX

**PII scrubbing**
- I include `rejectedValue` but scrub emails, card numbers, and long strings
- Raw values belong in audit logs, not in client responses

**Common mistakes**
- Serializing the raw `MethodArgumentNotValidException` — Jackson dumps a huge Spring-internal blob
- Using Spring Boot's default `{timestamp, status, error, path}` instead of a structured shape
- Treating Jackson deserialization errors as validation — they throw earlier as `HttpMessageNotReadableException` and should get their own `code: BODY_MALFORMED`
- Short-circuiting on first error — users rage-click
- Returning localized messages only — clients can't programmatically branch if the English version of the same constraint arrives the next day

**Testing**
- One MockMvc test per constraint; assert `Content-Type: application/problem+json`, each expected `errors[].field` and `errors[].code`
- New constraints added without tests are the classic regression
